items.content:
# Cursor plugins

Official Cursor plugins for popular developer tools, frameworks, and SaaS products. Each plugin is a standalone directory at the repository root with its own `.cursor-plugin/plugin.json` manifest.

## Plugins

| `name` | Plugin | Author | Category | `description` (from marketplace) |
|:-------|:-------|:-------|:---------|:-------------------------------------|
| `teaching` | Teaching | Cursor | Utilities | Skill mapping, practice plans, and learning retrospectives. |
| `continual-learning` | Continual Learning | Eric Zakariasson | Developer Tools | Incremental transcript-driven memory updates for AGENTS.md using high-signal bullet points only. |
| `cursor-team-kit` | Cursor Team Kit | Eric Zakariasson | Developer Tools | Internal team workflows for CI, code review, shipping, local automation, and verification. |
| `thermos` | Thermos | Cursor | Developer Tools | Thermo-nuclear branch review: deep security/correctness audits, harsh code-quality rubrics, parallel subagents, thermos orchestration, and optional merge-ready PR flows. |
| `create-plugin` | Create Plugin | Cursor | Developer Tools | Scaffold and validate new agent plugins. |
| `ralph-loop` | Ralph Loop | Cursor | Developer Tools | Iterative self-referential AI loops using the Ralph Wiggum technique. |
| `agent-compatibility` | Agent Compatibility | Cursor | Developer Tools | CLI-backed repo compatibility scans plus agents that audit startup, validation, and docs against reality. |
| `cli-for-agent` | CLI for Agents | Eric Zakariasson | Developer Tools | Patterns for designing CLIs that coding agents can run reliably: flags, help with examples, pipelines, errors, idempotency, dry-run. |
| `pr-review-canvas` | PR Review Canvas | Cursor | Developer Tools | Render PR diffs as review canvases grouped by importance. |
| `docs-canvas` | Docs Canvas | Cursor | Developer Tools | Render documentation as a navigable canvas. |
| `cursor-sdk` | Cursor SDK | Cursor | Developer Tools | Build apps, scripts, and automations with the TypeScript SDK. |
| `origin-apps` | Origin Apps | Cursor | Developer Tools | Skills for building on the Cursor Origin API. Fetch the live spec first, then follow the Origin rules for credentials, scopes, webhooks, paging, and errors. Includes a skill that plans the port of an existing GitHub App. |
| `orchestrate` | Orchestrate | Cursor | Developer Tools | Fan large tasks out across parallel cloud agents with planners, workers, verifiers, and structured handoffs. |
| `pstack` | pstack | Lauren Tan | Developer Tools | if you want to go fast, go deep first. pstack helps you write less, but higher quality code. rigorous agent workflows you can parallelize with confidence. |
| `dyl-stack` | dyl-stack | Dylan Gattey | Developer Tools | Dylan's agent style on top of pstack: root causes over symptom patches, The Algorithm before design, terse verified delivery, a PR review that fits in a paste, and Figma-to-UI with a visual judge. |
| `advisor` | Advisor | Cursor

items.content:
# /last30days

English | Français | Deutsch | Español | Português (Brasil) | 日本語 | 简体中文 | العربية | فارسی | Türkçe

 
   
 

 
   
     
   
   
   
     
   
   
   
     
   
 

**An AI agent-led search engine scored by upvotes, likes, and real money - not editors.**

This README tracks the current v4 pipeline. The runtime skill spec lives in skills/last30days/SKILL.md, which is the source of truth for the latest command and setup behavior.

**Claude Code (recommended — auto-updates via marketplace):**
```
/plugin marketplace add mvanhorn/last30days-skill
/plugin install last30days
```

**Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Gemini CLI, or any of 50+ Agent Skills hosts:**
```
npx skills add mvanhorn/last30days-skill -g
```
(`-g` installs globally for your user, available across all projects. Drop it to scope per-project.)

More install options (claude.ai web, OpenClaw, manual) in the Install section below.

Zero config. Reddit, HN, Polymarket, and GitHub work immediately, and so do patent filings and careers pages when your topic is a company. Run it once and the setup wizard unlocks X, YouTube, TikTok, arXiv, Techmeme, and more in 30 seconds.

---

Reddit upvotes. X likes. YouTube transcripts. TikTok engagement. Polymarket odds backed by real money and insider information. That's millions of people voting with their attention and their wallets every day. /last30days searches all of it in parallel, scores it by what real people actually engage with, and an AI agent judge synthesizes it into one brief.

Google aggregates editors. /last30days searches people.

You can't get this search anywhere else because no single AI has access to all of it. Google search doesn't touch Reddit comments or X posts. ChatGPT has a deal with Reddit but can't search X or TikTok. Gemini has YouTube but not Reddit. Claude has none of them natively. Each platform is a walled garden with its own API, its own tokens, its own auth. But you can bring your own keys and browser sessions, and suddenly an AI agent can search all of them at once, score them against each other, and tell you what actually matters.

That's the unlock. Not one better search engine. A dozen disconnected platforms, bridged by an agent.

```
/last30days Peter Steinberger
```

You have a meeting tomorrow. You Google them. You get their LinkedIn from 2023. /last30days gives you what they're actually doing this month: joined OpenAI to work on Codex, fighting Anthropic's ban on third-party agents, shipping 23 PRs at 85% merge rate, building "LobsterOS" for cross-device agent control, and r/ClaudeCode hit 569 upvotes debating whether he's a hero or "insufferable." Scattered across X posts, Reddit threads, YouTube transcripts, and GitHub commits. None of it was on Google.

## Why this exists

I built it to keep up in AI. Everything changes every day and the Reddit and X nerds are always on top of it first. I needed better prompts, and the training data was always months behind what the community had already figured out.

items.content:
# 

 Evaluate and improve AI agent skills and plugins: quality, security, overlap, compatibility, and real impact across agents 

[](LICENSE)
[](https://www.python.org/)
[](https://pypi.org/project/skillevaluator/)
[](https://docs.nvidia.com/skills/skillevaluator/repository-integration#copy-a-template)
[](https://docs.nvidia.com/skills/skillevaluator/)
[](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20614)
[](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/evaluating-ai-agent-skill-performance-with-nvidia-skillevaluator/)
[](https://github.com/NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator/stargazers)
[](https://github.com/NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator/forks)

 

> 📺 **Livestream:** Ask the Experts: Evaluating Agent Skills

SkillEvaluator checks AI agent skills and plugins, and measures a skill's effect
on task results: start with quality checks, then compare runs with and without a skill.

Catch skill issues before merge. Connect your repository to SkillEvaluator with a
CI template
for automated quality and security gates, without building or maintaining
evaluation code.

Agent skills are folders of instructions and supporting files defined by the
Agent Skills specification. SkillEvaluator is part of
the NVIDIA Verified Skills pipeline.

## Get started

Install the CLI in a Python 3.12–3.14 environment:

```bash
pip install skillevaluator
```

  Or use uv 

```bash
uv tool install --python 3.13 skillevaluator
```

 

For uv setup or direct GitHub source installation, see
Installation.

Then check skills from your terminal, CI, or agent:

   
 

   

Run checks backed by **500+ static rules and detection patterns**, without an
LLM key. Complete scanner setup
for full coverage:

```bash
skillevaluator validate \
  ./my-skill --tiers 1
```

  Run all three tiers 

After all-tier setup with NVIDIA Build,
remove `--tiers 1` to add deduplication and live agent evaluation to measure
skill lift:

```bash
skillevaluator validate \
  ./my-skill
```

 

 
 

   

Check every skill change. Run in your GitHub repo to open a setup PR:

```bash
skillevaluator ci init
```

Guided setup and CI templates for GitHub and GitLab.

 
 

   

Add the skill to Claude Code, Codex or another agent:

```bash
npx skills add \
  NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator
```

Then ask: *"Is my skill any good?"*
See the agent guide.

 
   

### ⚡ Harness check: will your agent load your skill?

🔑 **No API key** · 🤖 **No agent run**

```bash
skillevaluator harness-check ./my-skill
```

Illustrative summary of versioned profiles. Full output can include notes and schema diagnostics.

```text
╭─ Harness compatibility · my-skill ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│  ⚠️ codex        degraded    Description cut to 1,021 chars + '...' in the skill list   │
│  ❌ claude-code  not loaded  .agents/skills is not scanned                              │
│  ✅ opencode     loads                                                                  │
│  ✅ hermes       loads                                                                  │
│  ✅ openclaw

Now using node v20.20.1 (npm v10.8.2)

v20.20.1

#  🎻 PaperOrchestra: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated AI Research Paper Writing 
 Yiwen Song 1 , Yale Song 1 , Tomas Pfister 1 , and Jinsung Yoon 1  
  1 Google Cloud AI Research 
  

PaperOrchestra is a multi-agent framework for automated AI research paper writing. It flexibly transforms unconstrained pre-writing materials (ideas and experimental logs) into submission-ready LaTeX manuscripts, including comprehensive literature synthesis and generated visuals, such as plots and conceptual diagrams.

Acting like an orchestrated team of specialized agents, it handles outline generation, literature review, section writing, content refinement, and plotting to close the gap between raw research materials and submission ready papers.

 
   
 

## Key Features

- **Multi-Agent Pipeline**: Orchestrates specialized agents (Outline, Literature Review, Section Writing, Content Refinement, Plotting) for end-to-end paper generation.
- **Comprehensive Literature Synthesis**: Automatically searches, prioritizes, and integrates relevant literature into the manuscript.
- **Visuals Generation**: Generates plots and supports the inclusion of conceptual diagrams.
- **LaTeX Automation**: Produces submission-ready LaTeX manuscripts adhering to target conference templates.

## Installation

1.  **Environment Setup**: The project relies on a Conda environment named `paper_orchestra`. You can set up a similar environment with Python 3.11 and install the required dependencies.
    ```bash
    conda create -n paper_orchestra python=3.11
    conda activate paper_orchestra
    pip install -r requirements.txt
    ```

    # if you want to run demo and send emails to yourself at the end, set these 2 fields as well
    SMTP_EMAIL=your_email

    ```

items.title: 我司全面禁止 AI Coding，一夜之间回到古法编程时代
items.summary:
起因：
1. 部门某同事使用 AI 生成代码，审核不到位引发线上故障，导致大批量用户投诉。
2. 前一阵子另一同事删除不活跃用户数据，使用 AI 生成 SQL，结果误删部分活跃用户数据。
3. 叠加最近微软崩溃(Boss 认为是 Vibe Coding 导致)事故。

现状：

1. BOSS 对 AI Coding 失去信心，要求全面禁止 Vibe Coding ，AI 可以用于辅助分析、出方案，但是严令禁止直接生成代码，宁愿慢也不要出问题
2. 部分需求的 DDL 有所延长，但只相对于 vibe,古法编程所需耗时远远不够，还需要扯皮加时长 = =

---------

突然有点不适应，如果换成是你，你还能回归古法编程手搓代码吗？

在全面 Ai Coding 时代，如何限制 AI 才能减少类似问题发生，单纯的 review 或者工作流的限制能不能解决问题？

items.title: 求助帖：2 年被裁 3 次，简历花掉还能找到工作吗？
items.summary:
首先先自我介绍下吧，本人女，29 岁，未婚未育，河南小镇做题家出身，南航本（飞行器动力工程）+南大硕（环境工程），希望不要被熟人刷到

目前从事信贷风控行业，由于前期发育不完善，策略经验不足，在 2025-2026 年接连被裁 3 次，简历花掉，找工作都是已读不回，还有负债，压力山大。

等现在这家离职，马上就要没有收入了，我其实挺慌的

如果现在开始没有收入的话，差不多明年 2 月就要逾了吧，我不想逾

还是想请 v 站的朋友帮忙出出主意给些建议吧，我现在的这种情况怎么样才能搞到点钱？除了搞钱之外，也希望对我的未来有一些指点吧

到底是继续在风控领域找工作？还是副业？还是说考公考编？

一方面在想我是不是能继续在风控策略领域找工作？因为其实现在简历太花了，有人说这简历已经烂到可以直接丢垃圾桶的程度了；

另一方面，在想现在是不是可以搞搞副业，今年 vibecoding 出来一些东西，也就从网友兜里掏了几千块钱出来吧，但对于负债来说差太远了

比较坦诚的讲下被裁的原因，也希望 v 友能从各个角度给点建议：如果我有幸找到下一份工作，怎么才能保住下一份工作？

以及在此处插入一条求职，如果有合适的工作（什么样的都行，您觉得我能干的都可以），请联系我，我私发简历

**1）第一家**

在携程，数仓组--风控策略工程师（听组别和岗位就会奇怪吧，这里埋下了大雷），工龄 2.5 年，25.07 被裁

**岗位日常：** 给风控策略和模型同事打杂，负责策略和模型在内部引擎的上线；

**被裁原因：** **无核心业务资源+无数仓经验+无底牌**，就是那种感觉，要裁就是我了，是组里最没有用的那个人，别人要么做业务报表的开发，要么做模型特征的开发，但领导发现我只会打杂；

**能干 2.5 年的原因：** 有一定的 PYTHON 编程能力（其实很菜），挺被我的第一任领导赏识的，维护了一些模型和开发了一些提效工具（其实就是本人日常工作当中有一些痛点，感觉可以直接用代码解决，本人又懒，所以本人喜欢折腾一些提效工具），还升职加薪了；但是第二任领导来了之后就让我滚蛋了，因为我日常没什么产出，只是把模型部署上线。

**为后续埋大雷的地方：** 感觉在这边根本就没有建立起来自己的核心竞争力，既不会做风控策略，又不会做数仓，除了打杂就是打杂；

2）第二家

在美团，策略组--风控策略工程师，0.5 年

被裁原因：根据第一家公司的经历可以得知，我本人其实没有任何风控策略经验，所以并不能很好完成领导交代的任务，因而被裁

3）第三家

某家 500 强银行的金服公司，贷后策略，0.5 年；

被裁原因：个人能力问题+工作态度不行+有更便宜的人选（工作被应届生接受）

这次被裁，我自身有需要承担的责任。一方面，工作难度不大能 cover 住，但策略经验不足，前期交付的内容不够成熟，虽然之后有所改进，但没能扭转领导的印象；另一方面，对这边管理风格不满意，所以工作起来非常的心累，就会导致动作变形。

领导比较强势，经常当众骂人，我很难适应这种管理方式。所以被裁之后，除了焦虑，我其实也松了一口气。

这次被裁之前，其实我有预感，因为当时确实是感觉组里进了很多新人，又不可能全留，而且因为这里薪资低，男生很少，+1 和+2 私下小窗聊天说要招男生，接替我工作的就是一个应届的男生。

items.summary:
我今天重启了下电脑，重启前特意把 Claude 桌面版关了，但不知道为什么开启后 Claude 桌面版自动打开了，但这个时候我还没有开梯子，我都看到它显示“App Unavailable”了，感觉我离封号不远了

现在迭代那么快，上线后出问题再修。一般项目倒是无所谓，就怕一些不讲究的车厂也这么搞啊。 智驾 AI 传统 64 replies • 2026-11-19 15:41:02 +08:00 chaos93 7h 38m ago 6 1 如果汽车智驾的程序由 人 编写，你还敢用吗？ 请问 人 和 AI 的区别是什么？ 上线之前要不要测试的，AI 写的就不测试了？ PS： 以前我虽然也用 ai，但我一直不信任 ai 的代码，哪怕再耗时也会全部审阅一遍，这也导致我效率极低，部分时候比自己写还慢。 直到我领导开解我，他让我完成一个项目，也从来不会看我具体代码怎么写，只看最后项目能不能跑起来，把握大方向就行。 我可比 ai 笨，他都放心让我干，我为什么要一直怀疑 ai。 不要把 ai 和古法编程对立起来，把 ai 的提示词当做一门新的编程语言去使用，这门语言入门成本更低，上手更容易。 items.content: Fable 5.2 and Jagged AGI - by Ethan Mollick One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in Fable 5.2 and Jagged AGI General, often expert, and sometimes jagged Ethan Mollick Nov 09, 2026 1,476 233 172 Share Before getting started, I wanted to thank my readers for making my new book, Co-Existence, a New York Times bestseller two weeks in a row. If you haven’t read it, you can get a copy here . I have had the chance to use the new Claude Fable 5.2 quite a bit before its public launch 1 , and it is very impressive, following on the already excellent Opus 5.5. AI has gotten so good, in fact, that it is worth asking if Anthropic’s newest models (and the inevitable competing models OpenAI and Google will soon release) cross the boundary into being an Artificial General Intelligence? AGI is a much-debated term with a lot of potential definitions. For this post, I’ll go with: “an AI as good as most human experts at most intellectual tasks you can do with a computer.” This explicitly excludes a lot of human work, including interacting with the physical world and other people, as well as most actual jobs, where “using a computer” is just one task among many. Still, even with these caveats, building a limited form of AGI has long been the goal of AI developers. So as not to keep you in suspense, I think the answer is that this is “almost” AGI, or what I have called Jagged AGI. Even within my limited definition, there are still important areas in many tasks where AI is jagged enough to fall well behind human capability. But the jaggedness is no longer about simple errors or hallucinations, which makes it harder to describe. So I want to try to do that in this post by showing you what Fable can do and where the gaps are. To get started I asked the new model: “I write OneUsefulThing among other stuff, I need you to create the most impressive thing I can share with people when you launch. It needs to be embeddable in a post and i can preface it however you like. it needs to have a visceral impact on people to show what you can do and the range of capabilities. It should grab them quickly. Be amazingly clever about this.” Fable asked me not to reveal anything until you had watched its video to the end. This was in one shot, with no feedback from me beyond the prompt. There is creativity here (including in the twist ending) and judgment and playfulness and cleverness. This is, I think, at the level of a human expert trying to make a movie with code alone, the sort of performance I would once have associated with AGI. The “G” in AGI Code and video creation have been areas where AI development has focused, so is Fable 5.2 really a General Intelligence? Looking back across the gap between these books is a good way to get a sense of AI progress. And, thanks to AI, I can describe this progress with some quite lovely charts. Making the charts is itself a good indicator of how far things have come. In the era of chatbots, the era of Co-Intelligence , I would have had to work back-and-forth with an AI in a chat window, guiding it through each new step. In the current era of agentic AI that I cover in Co-Existence , I delegated the work and let the AI handle it. In this case, I used Opus 5.5 in Claude Projects, which allows you to talk to a single “orchestrator” agent that then spins off additional agents as needed, giving them instructions and relaying information back to you. Getting the work done was straightforward. I gave the AI a couple sentences of suggestions and it did what would have taken me hours of work (all the research, all the graphing, all the layouts, all the images, all the citations…) in minutes. And since I didn’t have to do the work, I had the AI make many options for me. I picked some and gave handwavy reactions to others that would drive a human team mad (“make it better”). It even caught that I’d gotten the math wrong. I was going to call this post “28 months on the exponential.” Some examples of interacting with Claude to make the graphics for this post. Notice that it corrected me. “This is the worst AI you will ever use” I wrote this in my last book on AI, and it has continued to be literally true at every moment since. From early 2023 through early 2024, there was a single AI model that was undeniably the best in the world: GPT-4 from OpenAI. This was the AI model that most people remember from the first couple years of AI use, it was the one I thought about while writing Co-Intelligence , and it was the one that gave ChatGPT its status as the default AI for many people. Since then, twenty different AI models have held the lead at one time or another, all from Anthropic, Google, or OpenAI. Which company had the best AI model in the world. But the changing lead alone hides an even bigger change. items.content: The Dot and the Swarm - by Ethan Mollick - One Useful Thing One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in The Dot and the Swarm Benefitting from the Bitter Lesson Ethan Mollick Oct 01, 2026 1,407 236 144 Share I generally think I have done a good job anticipating the direction and pace of AI over the few years I have been writing this Substack, but I think I recently got something fairly large wrong. In the last year I have been posting about how I suspected that humans would have to approach working with agents as a manager, deciding how to delegate work to agents and specifying how those agents should be organized. I thought that getting agents to work effectively as a group would take careful construction, akin to building a company, and that this would take time to figure out. Nope. I fell prey to The Bitter Lesson, the hard truth, learned over and over again, that things that we thought required elaborate human rules and thinking can be solved with the brute force of better machine learning systems and more AI. The Bitter Lesson is everywhere among AI startups and companies adopting AI. A huge amount of effort went into building elaborate computer systems to feed AIs the right information at the right time, but AI systems have learned to seek out information themselves. The same thing happened to prompting. People built elaborate templates and chains of prompts that walked the AI through a task one step at a time. Then newer models turned out to be better at planning the steps themselves, and, as our research shows , planning steps have much less value. The history of the Bitter Le— — you know what? I don’t really need to explain the Bitter Lesson, I asked Claude to do it in a music video. With one prompt, Fable wrote the lyrics and submitted it to Suno; Opus 5.5 did everything else using code alone without any image generation (How did Opus 5.5 pull this off? The Bitter Lesson tells you!). I gave no feedback at all. As somebody who teaches managers and has published research on management, I guess I believed that managing agents would be different. Humans have been working on management for a very long time without fully figuring it out. It seemed like the kind of thing that would need to be designed by people, at least for a while. It turns out that organizing work is just one more thing AI can learn to do. Which brings us to dots and Muse. Dots and Muse The number one app in the App Store right now is Meta’s Muse, a personal agent that promises to do work for you. OpenAI has now released a competitor tool, called dots. They aren’t alone: SpaceX’s Grok Bot, Instinct, and Gemini Spark all do similar things, more or less. All of these agents draw inspiration from a phenomenon you might remember from earlier this year, OpenClaw. items.content: Productiv-icky - by Ben Tossell - Ben's Bites Ben’s Bites Subscribe Sign in Productiv-icky Digging holes on the beach Ben Tossell Nov 17, 2026 75 3 1 Share productiv-icky (adj.) - the feeling of doing work you didn’t mean to do We have a problem. full interactive post is here We agree this is insane, right? Someone I don’t know sends me emails that I’m expected to reply to. I don’t know them. I don’t work for them. So I ignore them (well actually I send them to email jail). Nuh-uh, that’s not my work, buddy. But it’s different if it’s my super-intelligent, helpful agent friend… Yeses are easy. They’re quick. But every yes has a yes-tax. The hidden extra work you didn’t think of. The long tail of regret where you question why you ever said yes. Say I did reply to those emails, they’d send me stuff to read to show how great they are at their job and how much better I’d be. Then we’d organise a call (which would derail whichever day that call was on). Then we’d have follow-up items. Then a string of other crap I couldn’t care less about. I know what’s going to happen. I can smell it, it stinks. I’ve said yes and paid the tax many times before. Now I pay $200/mo for a super-intelligent, over-eager, needy little nerd to ping me incessantly about taking things off my plate. I feel bad for him. He wants to work. He’s gagging for it. Just. One. More. Task. Master. Plus, my little nerd has a gambling problem. Or rather, he feeds mine. Remember years ago sending tons of Slack messages to get the most out of your $20/mo plan? Nor me. Why? Because it’s dumb. But now we feel like we should use all our tokens before they run out. Why? Because everyone else is. We started measuring shovels instead of the hole. Someone’s needy little nerd booked their dentist, replied to their mum and launched a business whilst they were asleep. They’ve got an org chart. For nerds. With a Chief of Staff. You feel behind. Like way behind. So you grab a shovel and start digging. A little hole over there to triage your inbox, one here to draft your tweets, one to check on those. Then you spend your day checking the holes are being dug right. Before long, you’re surrounded by holes and a mountain of dirt you gotta do something with. Now as a man, holes are hardwired into my DNA. A few beers, a beach and a shovel, I’m digging a hole. I’d take pride in it. I’d make the best one, impressively round, deep enough to see sea water seep through the bottom. But I’d only dig one. There’s a whole beach but I chose this spot. Next time the needy little nerd pings you: do you really want another hole? Also, don’t dig big holes on the beach. They collapse. Nvidia still has the financial interests in supporting open models, which are to avoid concentration in power among a few customers who would develop their own chips and reduce Nvidia’s profits, but supporting the open ecosystem is a tricky puzzle more than an engineering problem to grind out a solution on. Nvidia’s business operations are famously extremely dependent on Jensen as an operator, so it is a consensus opinion that there are challenges ahead (or even more high-profile departures through chip-smuggling investigations or plain-old sharks circling more poachable talent). Nvidia’s number one goal is to stabilize the ship, deliver to customers in the next 24 months, and prevent implosion. Open models have been one of Jensen’s more ambitious, founder-style bets. These are crucial years for establishing use-cases, revenue flow, and motives to continue training the next generation models. The core of the argument is one upside for open models, a reason to be optimistic, and one downside. The positive case is that the open model economy has correctly latched onto “ownership of intelligence” and enterprise post-training as a crucial lane. What is to be determined is exactly how big the downstream market is.
